newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Failed round-world balloonists to try again.
newsitem.headline: Failed round-world balloonists to try again.

text.p: The two-man crew and engineers and sponsors behind a round-the-world balloon bid cut short by a fuel leak after only six hours said on Monday they would definitely try again, perhaps before the end of this year.
They told a news conference a new mission could be launched by their Swiss-Belgian-British team during the next winter "meterological window" from November to the end of March 1998.

"I think we can prepare for another effort by next year," said 39-year-old Belgian businessman Wim Verstraeten who took off on the fated flight on Sunday from the Swiss balloon centre of Chateau d'Oex with Swiss colleague Bertrand Piccard.

Jean-Bernard Maeder of the Swiss chronometer firm Breitling that financed the project told the news conference his company was "committed to the project of being the first to fly around the world in a balloon non-stop."
And Piccard, who earlier in the day spoke tearfully of "a stupid little technical problem" that had aborted the flight, said he would try again "even if 10 other people have done it already."
He said his wife Michele, who had given him an emotional send-off at Chateau d'Oex, had made clear she would not object.

The balloon, the Breitling Orbiter, came down in the Mediterranean off the southern coast of France after kerosene from fuel tanks leaked into the cabin slung underneath. Crew and cabin were rescued by the French navy.
Alan Noble, British chief engineer for the project, said it was not clear what had gone wrong.
"Before the take-off, I said that despite all the preparations the whole thing could be ruined by a five-franc valve," he said. "I have a horrible feeling that may just have been the case."
The capsule would be taken from France to Bristol, where it was built, in the next few days for full tests. "The damage is not too great. We may be able to use it again," said Noble.

British businessman Richard Branson, whose own bid to circle the globe in a balloon failed after just under 24 hours last Wednesday, has also said he will make another attempt later this year, possibly in November.

And an American millionaire, Steve Fosset, was understood to be preparing for a launch of his one-man Solo Challenger from St Louis in Missouri later on Monday. He failed in an earlier bid in February last year.
In an earlier interview at his Lausanne home, Piccard said he and Verstraeten were "very sad" at having to ditch when the flight had been going so well and the balloon "performing beautifully."
Piccard, from a famous family of explorers of the upper atmosphere and the ocean depths, told reporters at his home that only a "stupid technical problem" had forced the ditching.
The 48-metre (150-foot) high, helium-filled Breitling Orbiter took off in blue skies in conditions the mission team said were perfect for ballooning.

But just under an hour into the mission, heading over Lake Geneva at some 4,000 metres (12,000 feet), Piccard and Verstraeten noticed kerosene on the floor of the bright yellow gondola, which they wiped up with toilet tissue.

They then came down to around 2,000 metres (6,000 feet) to open the hatch of the pressurised capsule to throw out the paper and allow the fumes to escape. But after resuming their flight, the fuel began seeping in again.
"Our eyes were sore and our throats hurting from the fumes. Maybe it would have been possible to go on, but it would have been very, very dangerous," he said.
